[RAZI:107:5/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The severe threat concerns three acts—heedlessness about prayer, showing off, and withholding al-maʿūn—raising the question why sins that do not by themselves make one an unbeliever draw such punishment.
[RAZI:107:7/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · أبو بكر وعلي وابن عباس وابن الحنفية وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة والضحاك | reports | Abū Bakr, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk identify al-maʿūn as zakāt.
[RAZI:107:7/r10] RAZI, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ reports hearing an Arab use al-maʿūn for water and cites a line of poetry as evidence; the poet is not identified.
[RAZI:107:7/r11] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Water is plausibly singled out because it is a costly absence and cheap plenty; water is also the first request of Hell’s inhabitants and an early delight of Paradise. | mentions 7:50, 76:21
[RAZI:107:7/r12] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | A fourth explanation takes al-maʿūn as willing obedience, as in the expression about taming a camel until it gives obedience.
[RAZI:107:7/r13] RAZI, d. 606 · author | prefers | Rāzī prefers the broadest sense: every act of obedience that is easy to perform, because it yields more benefit.
[RAZI:107:7/r14] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Ostentatious prayer gives to people what belongs to God, while withholding al-maʿūn hides from people what is theirs—the hypocrites reverse both duties.
[RAZI:107:7/r15] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Asked why the unbeliever is not named, Rāzī answers that Adam’s lapse was mentioned only after his death and alongside repentance, as a lesson and as evidence of his elevated rank. | mentions 20:121
[RAZI:107:7/r16] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī closes by contrasting this sūrah about hypocrites with the next sūrah’s description of Muḥammad: the speakers seek pardon for falling short of the Prophet’s obedience without reaching the hypocrites’ evil.
[RAZI:107:7/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · أبي | reports | A report from Ubayy says reciting Sūrat Araʾayta earns forgiveness if the reciter pays zakāt, which is taken to suggest al-maʿūn means zakāt.
[RAZI:107:7/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The zakāt interpretation also fits the word’s placement immediately after prayer.
[RAZI:107:7/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · أكثر المفسرين | reports | Most exegetes say al-maʿūn is something ordinarily lent to rich or poor and not withheld without revealing vile manners, such as an axe, pot, bucket, fire striker, sieve, or adze.
[RAZI:107:7/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | A report says three things may not lawfully be withheld: water, fire, and salt.
[RAZI:107:7/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · أكثر المفسرين | reports | This customary lending includes letting a neighbor bake in one’s oven or leave belongings at one’s home for part of a day.
[RAZI:107:7/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | On this account, maʿūn derives from maʿn, a small thing; zakāt is a little taken from much, and familiar loaned utensils are likewise called maʿūn.
[RAZI:107:7/r8] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | This reading rebukes miserliness over small necessities as especially base; the hypocrites behaved this way, like those who hoard and urge others to hoard. | mentions 4:37, 68:12
[RAZI:107:7/r9] RAZI, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | The scholars commend keeping more household necessities than one needs so neighbors can borrow them, rather than giving only what is obligatory.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After discussing prayer, the passage follows by mentioning the withholding of aid.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | Scholars praise keeping extra household necessities to lend neighbors, rather than limiting oneself to the obligatory minimum.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra reports an Arab usage equating “al-ma'un” with water and cites the line “يمج بعيره الماعون مجا” as evidence.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Water may be singled out because it is most precious when absent and commonplace when present; people in Hell first ask for it, and it is among the first pleasures of Paradise. | mentions 7:50, 76:21
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A fourth view defines “al-ma'un” as willing obedience, as in the saying “restrain your camel until it gives you obedience.”
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر وعلي وابن عباس وابن الحنفية وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة والضحاك | reports | These authorities interpret “al-ma'un” as zakat.

[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Ordinary examples include letting a neighbor bake in one's oven or store belongings at one's home briefly.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Ma'un” is a diminutive thing, from “ma'n”; zakat is called this because a small fraction is taken from a larger holding, and customary borrowed tools also bear the name.
